articles.author: madhav kumar
articles.description:
Most online PDF mergers upload your file to a server. For sensitive documents, that's a problem.
Use pdf-lib in the browser:
Read files with File.arrayBuffer()


PDFDocument.load() each source
copyPages() into a new PDFDocument


save() and download via a Blob URL
The PDF never needs to leave the user's device for this flow.
Open DevTools → Network, merge a test PDF, and confirm there's no upload request carrying the file body. After the app loads, you can even try offline.
I packaged this (merge, split, and more) in PDFCraftify:
Merge tool: https://pdfcraftify.com/merge-pdf

Guide: https://pdfcraftify.com/guides/merge-pdf-without-uploading




  
  
  Tradeoffs



Browser memory limits very large jobs
Password-protected PDFs must be unlocked first
Not a replacement for full desktop DTP
If you build similar tools, what edge cases bite you most? Comments welcome.
articles.title: Merging PDFs in the browser with pdf-lib (no server upload)

articles.author: Kanishk
articles.description:
I got tired of wondering whether anything I read online was written by a person. So I built MadeByHumans (https://madebyhumans.diy), an experimental blogging platform with one rule: you literally have to type your posts by hand.
How the proof works: the editor listens to your typing. Rhythm, pauses, backspaces, corrections, all of it gets folded into an effort score for the piece. Pasting is capped at 100 words at a time and 300 total, so you can't just dump text into the box.
Then the fun part: readers can hit play on any post and watch a timelapse of the draft coming together. Every clumsy edit and second thought, visible by time of day. There's also an optional 60 second voice intro, and an embeddable badge that carries the effort proof to other platforms.
Honestly it started as a reaction to AI slop. But it turned into a more interesting question: what does "proof a human wrote this" even look like? Keystroke dynamics turned out to be a decent proxy. Nobody fakes their way through 300 words of backspaces and 2am rewrite sessions.
It's free, no ads, solo built, and real people are publishing on it already. Come poke around if you're curious.
Genuine question: does this read as convincing proof to you, or a gimmick? What would make you trust it?
articles.title: I built a blogging platform where you have to type every word by hand

Short answer: give every feature-flag poll a deadline shorter than the edge function's remaining lifetime, classify an intentional abort separately from transport failure, and keep serving the last validated snapshot. For a fintech pricing-rule rollout, page on sustained inability to refresh or on snapshot expiry, not on each timed-out poll. That preserves rollback control without turning a slow control plane into noisy customer-path alerts.
A timeout is not one event. It can be a caller deadline, platform termination, connection failure, slow response body, or a poll overlapping its successor. If all five become flag_fetch_failed, the graph looks busy while saying very little. Record the deadline source, elapsed time, snapshot age, evaluation result, and remaining invocation time.
